meters.label: B-tree bytes written for one 128 B event

frames.narration: A user event of 128 bytes arrives. In a B-tree it belongs in one specific 4 KB leaf page, found by walking root to leaf (3 page reads, the top two usually cached).

The B-tree changes the leaf in place and logs the change. The dirty 4 KB page is written back whole at the next checkpoint: 4 KB written for 128 B of data, up to 32x. In our simulation random writes average about 20x.
An LSM tree never edits a page. The same event is appended to the write-ahead log (sequential, for durability) and inserted into the in-memory memtable, which keeps keys sorted.

At 64 MB the memtable is written out in one sequential pass as an immutable sorted file (SSTable) with an index and a bloom filter. The memtable and its log segment start empty. After four flushes there are 4 overlapping files.
Read user:42. The memtable misses, so the engine checks the files newest to oldest. Bloom filters (about 1% false positives) rule out 3 of the 4 files from memory, so one data page is read.
Delete user:42. Nothing is erased: a tombstone is written like any other value. It hides the older value in the files, and takes up space until a compaction reaches the bottom.

Too many overlapping files make reads slow, so compaction merges the 4 files of 64 MB into one: newest version of each key wins, and tombstones are dropped once nothing older remains below. It rewrites about 256 MB to save future reads: that is the LSM write amplification.

Scan user:10 to user:20. The B-tree reads adjacent leaves (about 3 pages). The LSM tree must open every file whose range overlaps and merge them, and bloom filters cannot help a range. That is why scans favour the B-tree.
